ml_draft.text: ഇവിടെ പട്ടികപ്പെടുത്തിയ ഗുണങ്ങൾ ഒഴികെയുള്ളവ ആശ്രയത്തിന്റെ കാലത്തോളം നിലനിൽക്കില്ല — ദ്രവ്യം നശിക്കുന്നതിനു മുമ്പുതന്നെ അവ നശിക്കുന്നു. അതായത് അയാവദ്ദ്രവ്യഭാവിത്വം — ദ്രവ്യത്തിന്റെ ആയുസ്സിനു സമമല്ലാത്ത വൃത്തിയാണ് ഇവയ്ക്ക്.

en_simple_draft.text: The qualities other than those just enumerated do not last as long as their substrates: they are destroyed while the substance itself still exists. This is the *ayāvad-dravya-bhāvitva* — non-coevality with substance — that distinguishes them from the *yāvad-dravya-bhāvin* qualities.

literal_en:
The author now proceeds to point out the dissimilarity
of each of the. Qualities from another. Each of these Qualities
is related to the Generality of 'Colour' &c, and as such they
ct)me to be known as 'Colour', 'Taste' &c. That is to say, the
names 'Colour/ &c. constitute the point of dissimilarity of each
of the qualities from the rest
Some people hold that there is no such generality as
'Colour'. But this is not right. Because as a matter of fact,
we find that with regard to every one of the colours of blue, red
and the like, there is a common notion of 'Colour/—every one
of them being known as 'Colour/
Objection: "This common notion may be due to the
common character of being perceptible by the eye."
Reply: Not so ; that these are 'Colours' is not perceived
by the eye. If the notion of colour were due to the fact of
their being perceptible by the Eye, then that notion would
appear after their perception (while as a matter of fact, we find
them known as Colours at all times.)
Objection: "What is meant by * perceptibility by the
Eye* is the capability of being comprehended by the Eye; and
this capability continues to exist in Blue at all three points
of time (past, present and future)/'
Reply: That may be ; but as for that capability too,
if it were different with each individual Colour, then we could
not have any such comprehensive notion of them all as 'Colour';
as there would be no ground for any such comprehensive notion.
And if that capability be held to be common to all colours,
then there is only s difference in names (between our theory
and yours).

 228

PRAgASTAPÄDA BHÄSHYA-CHAP. VI.

The same argument holds as regards Taste and the other
qualities.

ml_draft.text: ഗുണങ്ങളുടെ ഭേദകത വർണ്ണിക്കാൻ ഗ്രന്ഥകർത്താവ് തുടരുന്നു. ഓരോ ഗുണവും — രൂപം, രസം, ഗന്ധം, സ്പർശം മുതലായവ — അതാതിന്റെ അപരസാമാന്യത്തിൽ (രൂപത്വം, രസത്വം, ഗന്ധത്വം ഇത്യാദി) സമവേതമായതുകൊണ്ടാണ് 'രൂപം', 'രസം' എന്നൊക്കെ വ്യവഹരിക്കപ്പെടുന്നത്. ചിലർ 'രൂപത്വം' സാമാന്യം ഉണ്ടെന്ന് നിഷേധിക്കുന്നു; ശ്രീധരൻ അതിനെ ഖണ്ഡിക്കുന്നു — നീലം, ചുവപ്പ് മുതലായ വർണ്ണങ്ങളിലെല്ലാം 'രൂപം' എന്ന സാമാന്യബുദ്ധി പ്രത്യക്ഷമാണ്; നേത്രേന്ദ്രിയഗ്രാഹ്യത്വം മാത്രമല്ല അതിന്റെ കാരണം.

en_simple_draft.text: The author now indicates the *vaidharmya* of the qualities. Each quality is named *rūpa*, *rasa*, etc., in virtue of inhering in a lower generality (*apara-sāmānya*) — *rūpatva*, *rasatva*, etc. Some opponents deny that *rūpatva* exists as a real *sāmānya*; Śrīdhara refutes them — the common notion of 'colour' across blue, red, etc., is itself perceived, and cannot be reduced to mere *cakṣur-grāhyatva* (perceptibility by the eye).

literal_en:
I
The author proceeds to describe Colour first, as it is |
Colour that is the direct cause of the manifestation or appear- f
ance of all things.
Among Qualities, Colour is perceived by the Eye alone, -j
and not by any other sense-organ.
Objection : -'In as much as the generality 'rüpatva also
is perceived by the Eye, how could perceptibility by the Eye
be regarded as the distinguishing quality of Colour ?"
Reply : Ail that we mean is that the said perceptibility
serves to distinguish Colour from- all other qualities: as the
word 'tatra,' ' of these \ distinctly refers only to the Categories under consideracion [i.e. Qualities, and 'rupatva* is
not a quality). As for generalities (like 'rüpatva'), Colour is
distinguished from these (which have no generalities) by the
fact of its having a generality.
Colour subsists only in Earth, Water and Light (Fire).
It makes perceptible the substance wherein it subsists, also
the Qualities, Action and Generalities pertaining to that substance. The colour of an object aids the £ye in the perception!
of that object.

 QUALITIES : SIMILARITIES AND DISSIMILARITIES.

229

Colour is eternal in the atoms of Water and Light. In
the atoms of earth it is destroyed by the contact of fire, as we
shall show later on.
The colour of all products is preceded (brought about)
by the colour of the object which is the material cause of those
products. The destruction of the Colour of the product is due
to the destruction of the object in which it subsists.
Objection: "We cannot admit that the destruction of Colour
follows upon the destruction of the object wherein it subsists; because as a matter of fact we find that the destruction
of the substance and its Colour is simultaneous."
Reply: It is not so ; because there is (at that time) no
cause for the destruction of Colour. In the case of the substance, the jar for instance, we find that when it is struck by
a club, there is produced a certain action among its constituent particles, and this action brings about the destruction of
the conjunction or cohesion of the particles forming the object;
and then follows the destruction of the object formed by that
cohesion, from the destruction of its cause (in the shape of
this cohesion). For the destruction of the Colour of that
substance, however, we find no cause at that time. If the
destruction of the Colour were to follow upon that of the
cohesion of the particles of the object, which cohesion is not
the cause of that Colour,—then, there would be a destruction
of the Colours of the earthenware fragments also. Hence we
consider it right to hold that it is the substance that is destroyed first, and after this destruction there follows the destruction of the Colour subsisting in that substance; and the
interval between the two destructions is so small that people
are led to regard them as simultaneous.
Some people regard the Colour and the Substance wherein it subsists to be identical, and hence they hold the cause
of the destruction of Colour to be the same as that of the
destruction of the Substance. To these persons the followiog

 230

PKACASTAPÄDA BHÄSHYA--CHAP. VI.

questions should be put:—Does the colour of the atom produce
another Colour or not ? When producing it, does it produce
it within the Colour itself, or in its substratum, the atom? If
it does not produce it, or if it produces it within itself, or in
the atom only,—then no Colour could be produced in the
Diad: and hence the whole world proceeding from that Diad,
would also be colourless.
Page 105] If on the other hand, the atom produces the Colour in the Diad, then in as much as nothing
that has not itself been brought into existence could be the
substratum of that produced Colour, this latter could be produced only after its substratum, the Diad, had been produced;
as no effect could ever be produced without a substratum«
Under the circumstances, how could these be any identity
between the two,—the two appearing one after the other ? |
Then again, you hold that it is only while the jar is existing |
that its Colour is destroyed by the contact of fire, and that it
is while the jar exists that the Colour is produced in it (by
the contact of fire). And there can be no identity between
two things, when the production of the one does not mean the
production of the other, and the cessation of the one does not 1
mean the cessation of another. Nor is it necessary that if
the two were different there would be a chance of their being ^
perceived apart from each other (which is not found to be the
case). Because Colour is always found to subsist in a substance. And as for this, it is the nature of things, and hence"
there is no good urging any serious abjections against it.

ml_draft.text: രൂപത്തെക്കുറിച്ച് ആദ്യം പറയുന്നു, എന്തെന്നാൽ വസ്തുക്കളുടെ പ്രകാശത്തിന്റെ പ്രത്യക്ഷ കാരണം രൂപമാണ്. ഗുണങ്ങളിൽ രൂപം മാത്രമേ കണ്ണുകൊണ്ട് പ്രത്യക്ഷമാകൂ. രൂപത്വം എന്ന സാമാന്യവും കണ്ണിനു ഗ്രാഹ്യമെങ്കിലും, അത് ഗുണവിഭാഗത്തിൽ പെടാത്തതുകൊണ്ടു 'തത്ര' എന്ന പദം കൊണ്ടു അതിനെ ഒഴിവാക്കുന്നു. രൂപം പൃഥിവി-ജല-തേജസ്സുകളിൽ മാത്രം വർത്തിക്കുന്നു. ജലത്തിന്റേയും തേജസ്സിന്റേയും പരമാണുക്കളിൽ അത് നിത്യം; പൃഥിവ്യണുവിലെ രൂപം പാകജം (അഗ്നിസംയോഗത്താൽ ഉത്പന്നം), ആശ്രയത്തിന്റെ നാശത്താൽ നശിക്കും. കാര്യദ്രവ്യത്തിലെ രൂപം കാരണത്തിലെ രൂപത്തെ പിന്തുടരുന്നു. — ദ്രവ്യവും രൂപവും ഒന്നുതന്നെയെന്നു വാദിക്കുന്നവർക്കു വിസ്തരിച്ച ഖണ്ഡനവും ശ്രീധരൻ ചെർക്കുന്നു.

en_simple_draft.text: The author treats *rūpa* (colour) first because it is the direct cause of the *prakāśa* (manifestation) of all objects. Of the *guṇa*s, *rūpa* alone is perceived by the eye. The generality *rūpatva* is also seen by the eye, but the word *tatra* ("of these") in the *bhāṣya* restricts the definition to qualities, excluding generalities. *Rūpa* subsists only in *pṛthivī*, *ap*, and *tejas*. In the *paramāṇu*s of *ap* and *tejas* it is eternal; in *pṛthivī*-atoms it is *pākaja* (produced by fire-contact) and destroyed with its substrate. The colour of a product follows the colour of its material cause. Śrīdhara also rebuts at length the view that *rūpa* and its substance are identical — distinguishing destruction of the substrate from destruction of the quality.

literal_en:
In the course of the treatment of each of the specific
qualities of perceptible substances, as are perceived by each
of the external organs of perception, it was necessary for our
author to describe Taste and Odour, after he had dealt with
Colour, which has the peculiarity of subsisting in more than
one substance; and he now proceeds to describe Taste.
Among qualities it is Taste alone that is perceived by the
Tongue; and it is by the Tongue alone that it is perceived.
It subsists only in Earth and Water.
'Jivana' is the substance of life. By 'pushfb i«? meant the
increase in constituent materials. 'Bala? is a peculiar Energy.
'Ärogya' is freedom from diseases. ^Of all these, Taste is the
cause, as may be learnt from works oh medicine.
The Taste subsisting in the Tongue aids in the perception of the Taste outside itself. It is of six kinds, sweet and
the rest,
Jusc as the Colour of the Earth-atoms is non-eteroal being
produced and destroyed by the contact of fire; while that of
the Water-atom is eternal; and the Cclour of the product is
preceded by a like Colour in the material cau.se; and is destroyed by the destruction of its substratum,—so exactly is
the case with Taste also.

ml_draft.text: ഓരോ ബാഹ്യേന്ദ്രിയത്താൽ ഗ്രഹിക്കപ്പെടുന്ന വിശേഷഗുണങ്ങളെ ക്രമമായി വർണ്ണിക്കാൻ വേണ്ടി, അനേകദ്രവ്യവൃത്തിയായ രൂപത്തിനു ശേഷം ഗ്രന്ഥകർത്താവ് രസത്തെ വർണ്ണിക്കുന്നു. രസം ജിഹ്വയ്ക്കു മാത്രം ഗ്രാഹ്യം; ജിഹ്വയ്ക്കു മാത്രമേ അത് ഗ്രഹിക്കാനാവൂ. പൃഥിവിയിലും ജലത്തിലും മാത്രമേ വർത്തിക്കൂ. 'ജീവന' (പ്രാണധാരണം), 'പുഷ്ടി' (അംഗവർദ്ധനം), 'ബല' (വിശേഷശക്തി), 'ആരോഗ്യം' (നിരാമയത്വം) എന്നിവയ്ക്ക് രസമാണ് കാരണം — ആയുർവേദത്തിലെന്നതുപോലെ. ജിഹ്വയിലെ രസം ബാഹ്യരസത്തിന്റെ ഉപലബ്ധിയിൽ സഹായിക്കുന്നു. പൃഥിവ്യണുവിലെ രസവും പാകജം, അനിത്യം; ജലാണുവിലെ രസം നിത്യം — രൂപത്തെപ്പോലെ.

en_simple_draft.text: *Rasa* (taste) alone among qualities is perceived by the tongue, and the tongue perceives nothing else. It subsists only in *pṛthivī* and *ap*. *Jīvana* (sustaining life), *puṣṭi* (growth), *bala* (a specific *vīrya*), and *ārogya* (health) all proceed from *rasa* — as the *āyurveda* tradition teaches. The *rasa* inhering in the tongue itself aids the apprehension of an external *rasa*. Six kinds — sweet, sour, salt, bitter, hot, pungent. As with *rūpa*: *rasa* in earth-atoms is *pākaja* and non-eternal; in water-atoms eternal; in products it follows the cause and is destroyed with its substrate.

literal_en:
[Page 106.] Odour alone is preceived by nose, and it is

 232

PKAQASTAPÄDA BHÄSHYA—CHAP. VI.

perceived by the nose alone. This restriction is based upon the
nature of odour. That is to say the nature of odour is such
that id is this alone that is perceived by the nose; there being
no declaration, either affirmative or negative, with legard to
such as are either seen or inferred.
The oJour subsisting in the nose aids it. It is of two
kinds—good and had odours. And just as Taste is produced
and destroyed in Earth-atoms by the contact of tire, and
in the product it- is preceded by the Taste in the material
cause, and is destroyed by the destruction of its substratum,—•
so exactly is the case with odour also. No tteruality belongs
to odour.

ml_draft.text: ഗന്ധം നാസികയാൽ മാത്രം ഗ്രാഹ്യം; നാസികയും ഗന്ധത്തെ മാത്രമേ ഗ്രഹിക്കൂ — ഇത് ഗന്ധത്തിന്റെ സ്വഭാവത്തെ ആധാരമാക്കിയ വ്യവസ്ഥയാണ്. നാസികയിലെ ഗന്ധം നാസികയ്ക്കു സഹായം. സുരഭി-അസുരഭി എന്ന് രണ്ടു ഭേദം. പൃഥിവ്യണുവിൽ പാകജം; കാര്യദ്രവ്യത്തിലെ ഗന്ധം മൂലദ്രവ്യത്തിലെ ഗന്ധത്തെ പിന്തുടരുന്നു; ആശ്രയനാശത്താൽ നശിക്കും. ഗന്ധത്തിനു നിത്യത്വം ഇല്ല — കാരണം പൃഥിവ്യണുവിലെ ഗന്ധം എപ്പോഴും പാകജമാണ്, അതുകൊണ്ട് രസത്തെപ്പോലെ ജലാണുവിലെ നിത്യഗന്ധം ഇല്ല.

en_simple_draft.text: *Gandha* (odour) is grasped by the nose alone, and the nose grasps only *gandha*. This restriction follows the *svabhāva* of *gandha*, not any other reasoning. *Gandha* inhering in the nose aids it. Two kinds — *surabhi* (pleasant) and *asurabhi* (foul). In earth-atoms *gandha* is *pākaja* and produced/destroyed by fire-contact; in products it follows the *gandha* of its cause and perishes with its substrate. There is no eternal *gandha* anywhere — unlike *rūpa* and *rasa*, since *gandha* belongs only to *pṛthivī* and even in its atom is *pākaja*.

ml_draft.text: ത്വക്കിന്ദ്രിയം — ചർമ്മത്തിലുള്ള ഇന്ദ്രിയം — കൊണ്ടു മാത്രമേ സ്പർശം ഗ്രഹിക്കാനാവൂ. പൃഥിവി-ജല-തേജസ്സ്-വായു — ഈ നാലിലും വർത്തിക്കും. ത്വക്കിന്ദ്രിയത്തെ സഹായിക്കുന്നു. രൂപത്തെ പിന്തുടരുന്നു — രൂപമുള്ളിടത്തു സ്പർശവുമുണ്ട്. ശീതം, ഉഷ്ണം, അനുഷ്ണാശീതം — മൂന്നു വിധം. കാഠിന്യം-കോമളത ഇവ പരമാണുവിന്റെ സംയോഗവിശേഷങ്ങളാണ്, വേറെ സ്പർശഭേദങ്ങളല്ല. നിത്യാനിത്യത്വം — ജലാണുവിലെ സ്പർശം നിത്യം; പൃഥിവ്യണുവിലെ പാകജം; ഗന്ധത്തിന്റേതുപോലെയല്ല, രസത്തിന്റേതുപോലെ.

en_simple_draft.text: The *tvak* or *tvac-indriya* — the *indriya* lodged in the skin — is what apprehends *sparśa* (touch). *Sparśa* exists in *pṛthivī*, *ap*, *tejas*, and *vāyu*. It aids the cutaneous organ. It follows *rūpa* — wherever there is colour there is also touch. Three kinds: cold (*śīta*), hot (*uṣṇa*), and neither-hot-nor-cold (*anuṣṇāśīta*). *Kāṭhinya* (hardness) and *mṛdutva* (softness) are particular kinds of conjunction of particles, not separate *sparśa* kinds. Eternality: like *rasa*, eternal in water-atoms; non-eternal (*pākaja*) in earth-atoms; not like *gandha* (which has no eternal form anywhere).

literal_en:
The author now proceeds to explain the process by which
the Colour &c. of the Earth-atom are produced and destroyed.
Though the 'Earth' itself is nothiug apart from the atoms, yet
the atoms are called 'parthiva' (of the earth), as compared with

en_simple_draft.text: Śrīdhara now unpacks the *pīṭhara-pāka* (jar-baking) sequence by which *rūpa* etc. arise and perish in earth-atoms. 'Earth' here means the *paramāṇu* that is the cause of earthy products. The *agni-saṃyoga* induces *karma* in those atoms, then *vibhāga*, then destruction of the prior *saṃyoga*, then destruction of the composite (e.g., the unbaked jar). On the now-disjoined atoms the heat of fire destroys the dark colour; further fire-contact, aided by the heat, produces the *pākaja* red colour in those same atoms. Then, through the *adṛṣṭa* of the experiencer-selves, fresh *karma* is set up in the now-coloured atoms, leading via *saṃyoga* to dvyaṇuka, tryaṇuka, ..., and finally to the new jar. The *rūpa* of the product is produced from the like *rūpa* of its *kāraṇa*. Crucially: production and destruction occur in the *paramāṇu*, not in the composite — because fire cannot pervade an undisrupted composite without destroying it. Śrīdhara then lists the many *kṣaṇa*s of the *pāka* sequence in elaborate detail; this is the famous *pīlu-pāka* vs. *piṭhara-pāka* debate-locus.

en_simple_draft.text: Number (*saṃkhyā*) is wellknown in form and existence, but some opponents (mainly Buddhist *vijñāna-vādin*s) deny it; Praśastapāda's *bhāṣya* on *ekādi-vyavahāra-hetuḥ saṃkhyā* targets them. The notion 'one, two, three,…' is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭa-buddhi*), and any qualified cognition presupposes a *viśeṣaṇa* — the quality called *saṃkhyā*. Śrīdhara refutes (a) the view that number-ideas are merely colour-ideas, by showing their forms differ from blue/yellow ideas; and (b) the Yogācāra view that they arise from *vāsanā* in the *ālaya-vijñāna*, by extending the same argument back onto blue-cognition. He then unpacks the *bhāṣya*'s two kinds — *ekadravyā* (in a single substance, eternal in water-atoms etc., non-eternal in products) and *anekadravyā* (from two upward). The famous account of *dvitva-utpatti* follows: from the conjoint cognition of two unities (*apekṣā-buddhi*) arises *dvitva-sāmānya-jñāna*, which both destroys the *apekṣā-buddhi* and produces *dvitva-guṇa-jñāna*; then arises the substance-cognition 'two substances'; then the *saṃskāra*; then destruction of the substance-cognition by the *saṃskāra*. The same sequence extends to *trika*, *śata*, *parārdha*, etc. Concludes: "Thus has Number been explained."

en_simple_draft.text: After *saṃkhyā*, the author turns to *parimāṇa* (dimension/measurement). *Parimāṇa* is the quality that underlies the *vyavahāra* of recognising and naming a thing's smallness (*aṇu*), largeness (*mahat*), length (*dīrgha*), shortness (*hrasva*). Four kinds. *Mahat* is twofold: eternal (the supreme magnitude of *ākāśa*, *dik*, *kāla*, *ātman*) and non-eternal (in *tryaṇuka* and upward). *Aṇu* likewise twofold: eternal (*pārimāṇḍalya* in *paramāṇu* and *manas*) and non-eternal (in *dvyaṇuka*). *Dīrgha*–*hrasva* attach to caused *mahat*–*aṇu* respectively. Non-eternal *parimāṇa* has three causes: *saṃkhyā*, *parimāṇa* (of components), and *pracaya* (loose vs. dense aggregation). The *dvyaṇuka*'s *aṇutva* comes from the duality of its two *paramāṇu*s; the *tryaṇuka*'s *mahattva* from the *tritva* of its three *dvyaṇuka*s (by *Īśvara*'s will). Two cotton-balls rolled into one show *pracaya* as a distinct cause: same *saṃkhyā* and *parimāṇa* of parts but different result. *Mahattva* differs from *dīrghatva*, *aṇutva* from *hrasvatva* — directly perceptible to *yogi*s in atoms and dyads. All four kinds, being caused, perish with their substrate.

 QUALITIES : SIMILARITIES AND DISSIMILARITIES.

Having thus pointed out the similarity of Isolation with

between uhese two.—Etdvän &c. Isolation differs from number

sub-classes 'one', 'two', &c. under the one general class of

Question: "How is it then, that there are intermediate
class-notions with regard to the ' single Isolations ' belonging to
many substances ? "
Answer : 'Thi3 one is separate' 'these two are separate',—
in all these cases when separateness or Isolation is spoken of, it
is always spoken of as qualified by Number. The Isolation
inhering in a single substance is qualified by the number 'one';
and it is a peculiar form of this number which appears to be
spoken of as a 'sub-class'; and as for the comprehensive notion of
'Isolation', it is due to the class or generality of 'Isolation', and
not to any sub-classes of it.
In the'same manner we should also deny any such generality
or class as 'atom\ inhering in all atoms ; as also universal usage
may be explained as based upon the generality 'anu' as qualified by the epithet lparama\
Question : "Why do you not admit that a single Isolation
exists in all substances, and that the diversity of notions is due
to the qualifying number, 'one', 'two' &c. 1"
Answer: We do not admit this for the simple reason
that in the case of substances produced one after the other, we
do not perceive any inherence of qualities, as we do that of the
Generalities. Nor could it be a Generality or Class itself; as
until ideas of other substances are present, there is no notion of
Isolation, just as there is none of any Generality.

en_simple_draft.text: Why is *pṛthaktva* (separateness) discussed before *saṃyoga*/*vibhāga*? Because, like *saṃkhyā* and *parimāṇa*, it inheres in substances across all three triplets (earth/water/fire and *ātman* etc.), whereas *saṃyoga* etc. are more restricted. *Pṛthaktva* is the *guṇa* underlying the usage "this is *anya* (different) from that." Although a mere *anyonyābhāva* (mutual negation) might suffice to ground the usage, the Vaiśeṣika — which does not yet (here) admit *abhāva* as a *padārtha* of comparable footing — posits *pṛthaktva* as a positive *guṇa*. Three sub-kinds: *eka-pṛthaktva*, *dvi-pṛthaktva*, *tri-pṛthaktva* — paralleling number. *Dvi-pṛthaktva* etc. arise from *apekṣā-buddhi* in the same way as *dvitva*. Eternality/non-eternality runs parallel to *saṃkhyā*.

en_simple_draft.text: *Saṃyoga* is the *prāpti* (attainment of contact) of two previously-unattained substances. The *bhāṣya* defines it as *aprāptayoḥ prāptiḥ*. Śrīdhara probes the famous *kapi-vṛkṣa-saṃyoga* (monkey-on-tree) problem: where does the conjunction inhere — in the part where the monkey grasps, in the whole tree, in both? — concluding that *saṃyoga* is *avayavavṛtti* (partial), but with intricate qualifications. Three kinds: (i) *anyatara-karma-ja* (caused by motion in one relatum, like the bird landing on the still post), (ii) *ubhaya-karma-ja* (motion in both, like two fighting rams), (iii) *saṃyoga-ja* (born of a prior conjunction, e.g. one's hand touches another's because one's body has moved into contact). The *vibhu* substances (*ākāśa*, *dik*, *kāla*, *ātman*) admit only *saṃyoga-ja*, having no *karma*. The corporeal (*mūrta*) substances admit all three. *Saṃyoga* is the chief *asamavāyi-kāraṇa* of caused substances. Special destructive conjunctions — *nodana* (urging) and *abhighāta* (impact) — generate motion and *vega*.

en_simple_draft.text: After *saṃyoga* comes *vibhāga* — the disjunction of what was previously conjoined. *Vibhāga* is the *guṇa* underlying the *vyavahāra* 'they have separated.' Like *saṃyoga*, it has three sub-kinds: *anyatara-karma-ja*, *ubhaya-karma-ja*, and *vibhāga-ja* (from a prior disjunction). The *vibhāga-ja* analysis is the engine of the destruction-sequence of caused substances: *karma* in one *avayava* produces *vibhāga*; this *vibhāga* destroys the *saṃyoga* that held the composite together; that destruction destroys the *avayavin* (composite); and a new *avayava-saṃyoga* with another body simultaneously arises. Śrīdhara discusses *vyāpyavṛtti* / *avyāpyavṛtti* questions about *vibhāga*, the asymmetries between the *avayava-vibhāga* and the *kārya-avayava-saṃyoga*, and the cosmic *pralaya*-disjunction set up by *Īśvara*'s will.

en_simple_draft.text: *Paratva* (priority) and *aparatva* (posteriority) are each twofold — *dik-kṛta* (space-based) and *kāla-kṛta* (time-based). The *dik-kṛta* underlies the usage 'this is far, this is near' between coexistent substances; the *kāla-kṛta* underlies 'this is *jyeṣṭha* (senior), this is *kaniṣṭha* (junior).' Like *dvitva*, they arise from *apekṣā-buddhi*: when the observer cognises the *dik-saṃyoga*s of two trees with himself, and these differ in *parimāṇa* (extent), the *apekṣā-buddhi* gives rise to *paratva* and *aparatva* in the further/nearer tree respectively. For *kāla-kṛta*, the engine is the difference in the *parimāṇa* of solar revolutions intervening. These *guṇa*s are practical (*vyāvahārika*) and inhere in the relata, since *dik* and *kāla* themselves are *eka-nitya-vibhu* and cannot host such distinctions.

en_simple_draft.text: Having shown that *paratva*/*aparatva* (and the proximity-distance pair) arise from *buddhi*, the author now turns to consider what this *buddhi* is. The words *buddhi*, *upalabdhi*, *jñāna*, *pratyaya* are *paryāya* — synonyms for the same *ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*. The Sāṃkhya *buddhi* is the *mahat-tattva* — an evolute of *prakṛti*, the seat of *adhyavasāya*; that doctrine is rejected here. For Vaiśeṣika, *buddhi* is *pratyartha-niyata* — one cognition per cognized object — and is produced in the *ātman* by *manas*-contact with it. *Upalabdhi*, *jñāna*, *pratyaya* are mere synonyms, picking out the same *guṇa* under different aspects. Śrīdhara refutes the Sāṃkhya view that the *jñātṛ* (cogniser) is identical with *jñāna*, and the Buddhist *vijñāna-vāda* that takes the *jñāna-santāna* as ultimate.

en_simple_draft.text: The author now signals the manifold subdivision of *buddhi* and explains why its varieties are endless. The clause "and it appertains to its respective object" is added to support the principle of *pratyartha-niyata-buddhi* — one *buddhi* per cognised *artha*. Because objects are endless in variety, *buddhi* too is endless; this is the underlying reason for the proliferation of *jñāna*-kinds about to be laid out (*vidyā*, *avidyā*, and their sub-kinds).

en_simple_draft.text: Though *buddhi*s are as numerous as there are objects in the world, two main divisions suffice: *vidyā* (knowledge) and *avidyā* (ignorance/error). *Vidyā* is a *niścaya* — a definite cognition free from *saṃśaya* (doubt), *viparyaya* (misconception), and *anadhyavasāya* (indeterminate cognition) — and reveals its *prameya* as it really is. *Avidyā* is the contrary — like darkness in being not the real revelation of the object. *Vidyā* is fourfold: *pratyakṣa*, *anumāna* (i.e., *laiṅgika*), *smṛti* (recollection), and *ārṣa* (the *vidyā* of seers). *Avidyā* is fourfold: *saṃśaya*, *viparyaya*, *anadhyavasāya*, *svapna* (dream). Śrīdhara at length defends this restriction against opponents who would add *śabda*, *upamāna*, *arthāpatti*, *anupalabdhi*, etc., as independent *pramāṇa*s, showing each can be reduced to *pratyakṣa* or *anumāna* (or to the testimony of *śabda* which itself is a kind of *anumāna* via *śābda-bodha*).

en_simple_draft.text: *Saṃśaya* (doubt) is defined widely. When between two well-known objects (e.g. *sthāṇu* and *puruṣa*) — each carrying many *viśeṣa-dharma*s — the *viśeṣa*s of the perceived object are not seen (only what is *sādhāraṇa* to both is seen, e.g., the upright shape), and the *viśeṣa*s of the contrary object are also not seen, but only remembered as previously cognised — then a wavering, oscillating cognition arises: "Is this the *sthāṇu* or the *puruṣa*?" The mark of *saṃśaya* is this back-and-forth swing, lacking *niścaya*. Śrīdhara identifies the *sādhāraṇa-liṅga-darśana* and the bilateral *viśeṣa-asmṛti* as the two principal *hetu*s of doubt.

en_simple_draft.text: After *saṃśaya*, Praśastapāda treats *viparyaya* (misconception/erroneous cognition). *Viparyaya* too pertains to perceptible and inferable objects, since Vaiśeṣika admits no third *pramāṇa* of veridical knowledge. Perceptual *viparyaya*: e.g., perceiving a horse for the cow, or vice versa. The cause-structure is: the *indriya* deranged by *vāta–pitta–kapha* fails to grasp the *viśeṣa-dharma* of the real object; meanwhile the *ātma-manas* contact, charged by a *saṃskāra* from a prior cognition of the misperceived object, and aided by *adharma*, produces "this is the horse" of the cow. Inferential *viparyaya*: vapour mistaken for smoke, then fire inferred from the supposed smoke; or *gavaya*-horns sighted leading to inferring 'cow'. Śrīdhara also includes (per Praśastapāda): mistaking heterodox doctrines (the *bauddha*, the *jaina*) for *śreyas*; the false *ātma*-cognition in *deha*/*indriya*/*manas*; the cognition of eternality in non-eternal things; the cognition of effect-production without an adequate cause. Crucially, Śrīdhara identifies the Vaiśeṣika position as *viparīta-khyāti* (cognition of the contrary) and at length rebuts *asat-khyāti* (Mādhyamika), *ātma-khyāti* (Yogācāra), and *anirvacanīya-khyāti* (Advaita).

en_simple_draft.text: The word *api* ("also") signals that *anadhyavasāya* (indeterminate cognition), like *viparyaya*, attaches to both perceptible and inferable objects. *Tāvat* defers the inferable kind to later. For perceptible familiar objects, *anadhyavasāya* arises from inattention or further-knowledge-desire — e.g., a well-known king passes by but the observer, distracted, has only "someone has gone by," not grasping the king's *viśeṣa*. For unfamiliar perceptible objects, e.g. an inhabitant of the Daksha-country before a *panasa* (jackfruit) tree, who has many *niścaya*s about it (existing, *dravya*, modification of *pṛthivī*, *vṛkṣa*, with such a colour, with branches) and even grasps the *panasatva*-class abstractly, but lacks the specific name *panasa* — until someone tells him. For inferable objects, an inhabitant of the Nārikela continent, having no *gavaya*-acquaintance, sees an unknown animal and stops at "this is some kind of animal," unable to determine the *jāti*. Śrīdhara distinguishes *anadhyavasāya* from *saṃśaya*: the latter swings between two definite alternatives, the former simply lacks distinct cognition of *viśeṣa*; nor is it *vidyā*, since it does not give rise to *pravṛtti*.

en_simple_draft.text: Now *svapna* (dream cognition). When the *indriya*-group has ceased to function (*uparatendriya-grāma*) and the *manas* has retired into the heart-region of the *ātman* (*pralīna-manaska*), then — through the *adṛṣṭa*-induced *prāṇa-apāna* breathings, the special *saṃskāra* called *svāpa* (a particular state of *ātma-manas-saṃyoga*), and prior cognitive *saṃskāra*s — there arises through the *manas* (not the sense-organs) a cognition resembling direct *pratyakṣa* but with reference to *asat* objects. Three kinds: (1) *saṃskāra-prabalatva* — the lover dreaming of the beloved; (2) *dhātu-doṣa* — *vāta*-dominant body flying in air, *pitta*-dominant entering fire, *kapha*-dominant crossing oceans; (3) *adṛṣṭa* — auspicious or inauspicious dreams of utterly unknown objects, generated by *dharma* and *adharma*. All three are species of *viparyaya*, but classified separately because confined to a particular bodily state. The *svapnāntika* cognition ("I have been dreaming of such-and-such") is a form of *smṛti* but occurs in the *uparatendriya* state, so the author flags it. *These are the four kinds of avidyā.*

The author proceeds to explain the definition of ' sensuous

fact of being produced out of the barley-seed serves as a definition of the barley-sprout; by which reason too this latter name
is given to it.

section on ' Buddhi '; and is thereby so qualified as not to
extend to pleasure, &c. That is to say, the sense of the definition is that that' cognition * which appears after contact with
sense-organs is ' sensuous perception.' And it is a well-known
fact that pleasure <&c, have not the nature of ' cognition'; and
äs such, how could the definition apply to these ?

due to their inherence in something inhering in that which is

due to inherence (in the sense-organ); (5) that of ' gabdatva'
is due to its inherence in that which inheres in the sense*
organ; (6) and that of negation is due to its qualifying that which
is related to the sense-organs; these are the six kinds of

* sense-contact \ There are certain perceptions of negation,—
such for instance as (a) the perception of the absence of taste
&c, in colour, which is due to its qualifying that which inhere«
in a thing in contact with the aense-orgun; (6) that of the
negation of * rasatva' (fee, in ' riipatva,' which is due to its

iu general).
Some people regard either Conjunction only or Inherence
only as the cause of perception ; and they deny the intervening

The nature of things is such that they are perceived only
through contact with something eise (the sense-organs); as for
the possibility of confusion and uncertainty of perception, it is
obviated by the restriction or limitation due to the proximity
of their substratum.
Recapitulation: Such is the perception of us, who are not
Yogis. The author proceeds to describe the ' sensuous cognition* of the Yogis: As for those that differ from us <itc.t by
' y°9a ' here we mean ' ecstacy •/ and it is of two kinds the
Conscious or Concrete and the Unconscious or Abstract. The
* concrete ecstacy ' consists in the contact of the mind, which
has been controlled and concentrated upon a> portion of
the self, with the self in whom there is a desire for knowledge ;
and the * Abstract ecstacy ' consist, in the contact without any
end in view, of the controlled' mind with a part of the self
arising from ' non-rising' or undisturbed state of the mind.

Of these two, the latter belongs to the seeker after deliverance,
and serving the purpose of dissipating ignoruuce, comes to be
fully developed in the last life of the^'ira upon earth ; it does not

any external object, being centered in the self alone; the former
(concrete) ecstacy on the other haud, is always aided by a
certain desire, and as such brings about dharma ; and it always
illuminates that external object with regard to which there is ill
the mind a desLe tu know the truth. These are the two kinds
of ecstacy or yoga; and those who have once experienced this
ecstacy, arft called 'yogis* even wheri they have fallen of from
that couditiou ; because of the capability in them (of returning
to the same couditiou).
Inasmuch as the yogis have no perception of supefsenBuous objects, until the covering of impurities have bt^en removed from thier minds, the author adds that while in the
state of ecstacy, by means of their iuiu<is helped by dharma

to. their own selves as well as bo those of others, and also with regard to akägci (space), time, air, atoms, minds, the qualities belonging to the last two, ami inherence. By ourselves the self is

natural form of the self is perceived by tue yogis, alone. When
the yogi makes ur his mind to know the true character of the

mmd from tbe external sense-organs, aud fixing it upon a definite part of the self he continues one-pointedly to practise

meditation upon the self; and then there coming into manifestation such of his dharma as tends to the accomplishment of
his true knowledge, there clearly appears before his mind the real

These arguments have elsewhere been put in the form of

mension. [And the true knowledge of self &c. would be those

Objection: " In the case of water that is being heated we
find that there are varying grades of heat; and yet we never

highest limit); nor do we ever perceive any limit upon the
practice of jumping; as there is no man that can jump over all
the three worlds (and until this limit is reached there would
always be varying grades of jumping)."
Reply: When a property that has a permanent substratum
produces a peculiarity in its subtratum, a practice or repitition which would be of the nature of such a property would,
gradually, reach the highest limit of excellence ; as for instance when gold is repeatedly heated and treated by the method
of 'putapaka' its purity gradually reaches the highest limit
in acquiring the character of the raktasdra (V). As for the
htating of tv.iter, it has got no permanent substratum, wherein
reptetion could bring it up to the highest limit; this absence
of the permanent substratum is proved by the fact of the water
entirely disappearing on the application of great heat. Then
as for the practice of jumping, it is not productive'of any peculiarity in its substratum ; because the first jumping having been
totally destroyed, leaving no traces behind, the second aud
subsequent j um pings might be the effects of other forces and
efforts, like an altogether new jumping-{and hence any susequent

previous jumping). It is for this reason that we find that when
the man is tired by three or four jumps, his limit of jumping

this could not be if practice brought about gradual improvenveot). As for buddhi on the other hand, it has a permanent
substratum, aud briugs about peculiar characters iu its
substratum ; as we find that though something may not be
comprehended at first, it becomes duly comprehended, when the
buddhi is repeatedly applied to it, And thus the previous repitition always producing a higher peculiarity in it at each step
of the practice, when the practice is kept up continuously and
with great care for a long time, the buddhit having obtained
fresh force due to dhwma born of yoga, must reach its highest
limit; and there is nothiog unreasonable or improbable in this.

en_simple_draft.text: Śrīdhara opens the longest *gloss* of this chapter — on the definition of *pratyakṣa*. *Akṣa* here is the *indriya*; that which is produced upon (*pratītya*) the *indriya* is *pratyakṣa*. The peculiar cause distinguishes it from cognitions of similar and dissimilar classes, like *yavāṅkura* (barley-sprout) being defined by its origination from the barley-seed. Objections that pleasure, pain, *saṃskāra* are also sense-born are dismissed: the definition is contextually restricted to the *buddhi* chapter. *Saṃśaya* and *viparyaya* are excluded by the section being on *vidyā*. *Prameya*s: *dravya*, *guṇa*, *karma*, *sāmānya* — *viśeṣa* and *samavāya* are not directly grasped by an *indriya*. *Pramātṛ* = *ātman*; *prameya* = *dravyādi*; *pramiti* = the resultant *jñāna*; *pramāṇa* = the *catuṣṭaya-sannikarṣa* (the fourfold contact: *ātman*–*manas*, *manas*–*indriya*, *indriya*–*viṣaya*, plus the *viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya* qualification-contact). Six *indriya*s — refuting the Sāṃkhya eleven. The *savikalpaka* / *nirvikalpaka* dispute: the determinate cognition presupposes an indeterminate one, since the name-remembrance triggered by the determinate cognition itself presupposes prior cognition of the form. *Yogi-pratyakṣa* via *yoga-ja-dharma*-empowered *manas*: in the *yukta* state, all *ātman*s, *ākāśa*, *dik*, *kāla*, *paramāṇu*, *vāyu*, *manas*, their *guṇa*-*karma*-*sāmānya*-*viśeṣa*, and *samavāya* are directly intuited; in the *viyukta* state, *sūkṣma*/*vyavahita*/*viprakṛṣṭa* objects become accessible via fourfold contact aided by *yoga-ja-dharma*. *Pramāṇa* is the contact, not the *jñāna*-*phala*. Production-conditions of substance-*pratyakṣa*: *aneka-dravyavattva* (many-parts-character), *udbhūta-rūpa-prakāśa* (manifested colour), *catuṣṭaya-sannikarṣa*, and the auxiliaries *dharma*, *adharma*, *deśa*, *kāla*. The *Sāṅkhya* objection that this would entail perception of *viśeṣa* alongside *sāmānya* is met by the *aneka-dravyāśrayatva*-criterion. This is one of the most extensive *ṭīkā* sections on Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika *indriya-pramāṇa-vāda*.

en_simple_draft.text: *Darśana* in the *bhāṣya* means *grahaṇa* or *jñāna* — the cognition of the *liṅga*; it is not restricted to visual perception. The reason: a previously-inferred *liṅga* can itself trigger a further inference, where the *darśana* is itself an inference. The seeing of a *liṅga* also produces a *saṃskāra* of it, but that is not the *bhāṣya*'s referent here — the section being on *buddhi*. The prefix *sam* in *sañjāyamāna* means *avitatha* (truly, rightly), and serves to exclude *saṃśaya*, *viparyaya*, and *smṛti*: doubt and misconception are already excluded by the section being on *vidyā*; the *sam* additionally excludes *smṛti*, since *smṛti* depends on a prior cognition and not on a present *liṅga*-cognition of a real object.

en_simple_draft.text: Praśastapāda now defines the *liṅga* (probans/inferential mark). The *anumeya* is the *dharmin* qualified by the *sādhya-dharma*. A *liṅga* is that which (a) is related to (resides in) the *anumeya*, (b) is known to exist in *sapakṣa* (instances connected with the *anumeya*-class), and (c) does not exist in *vipakṣa* (instances where the *sādhya* is absent). This is the famous *trairūpya*. Deviation from any of these three yields *viruddha* (counter-vailing), *ajñāta* (unestablished), or *sandigdha* (doubtful) — none of which is a true *liṅga*. So says Kāśyapa (the *sūtra*-author Kaṇāda). Śrīdhara notes that even partial *vipakṣa-vṛttitva* (*vipakṣaikadeśa-vṛtti*) disqualifies the mark.

ml_draft.text: ഭാഷ്യാർത്ഥം ഗ്രന്ഥകർത്താവ് വിശദമാക്കുന്നു. (1) അനുമേയസംബന്ധിയിൽ കാല-ദേശത്തിലോ കാലത്തിലോ ദേശത്തിലോ വർത്തിക്കുന്നത് — ഇത് ലിംഗത്തിന്റെ പ്രഥമലക്ഷണം. ഉദാ: ധൂമം-അഗ്നി; ധൂമം അഗ്നിയോടു സകാല-സദേശവൃത്തി. കാലവൃത്തി-ഉദാഹരണം: കാർത്തികനക്ഷത്രോദയം — രോഹിണിയുടെ കാലവൃത്തി. ദേശവൃത്തി — സമുദ്രജലത്തിന്റെ വൃദ്ധി — ചന്ദ്രോദയത്തിന്റെ ദേശവൃത്തി. (2) അനുമേയത്തിന്റെ കാര്യം — അനുമേയത്തിന്റെ കാര്യഭൂതലിംഗത്തിൽ നിന്നു അനുമേയത്തെ അനുമാനിക്കാം (ധൂമത്തിൽ നിന്ന് അഗ്നി). (3) അനുമേയത്തിന്റെ കാരണം — അനുമേയത്തിന്റെ കാരണഭൂതലിംഗത്തിൽ നിന്ന് അനുമേയം (മേഘഗർജ്ജനത്തിൽ നിന്ന് വൃഷ്ടി). (4) സംയോഗി — സംയോഗത്തിലുള്ളവയിലൊന്നു മറ്റേതിന്റെ ലിംഗം. (5) സമവായി — സമവായസംബന്ധികളിലൊന്ന് മറ്റേതിന്റേത്. (6) വിരോധി — വിരോധികളിലൊന്നു മറ്റേതിന്റെ അനുപലബ്ധിയിലൂടെ ലിംഗം. അന്വയ-വ്യതിരേക-വ്യാപ്തി, പ്രതിജ്ഞാ-ഹേതു-ഉദാഹരണ-ഉപനയ-നിഗമനങ്ങൾ — ന്യായാവയവചർച്ച. അന്വയിന്, വ്യതിരേകിന്, അന്വയ-വ്യതിരേകിന് — ലിംഗത്രയം. വൈശേഷികസിദ്ധാന്തത്തിലെ അനുമാനവ്യാപ്തിക്രമം — സ്വാർത്ഥാനുമാന-പരാർത്ഥാനുമാന-ഭേദമടക്കം — സമഗ്രമായി.

en_simple_draft.text: Śrīdhara now unpacks the *bhāṣya*'s sub-classification of the *liṅga*. (1) That which is *sāmānādhikaraṇya*/co-located with the *anumeya* in time and place, or in time only, or in place only — e.g., smoke with fire (both); the rising of *kṛttikā* as *liṅga* for rohiṇī (time-only); ocean-tide as *liṅga* for the moon (place-only). (2) The *kārya* of the *anumeya* — inferring fire from smoke. (3) The *kāraṇa* of the *anumeya* — inferring rain from cloud-thunder. (4) *Saṃyogi* — one of two conjoined items as *liṅga* of the other. (5) *Samāvāyi* — one of two inherence-related items as *liṅga* of the other. (6) *Virodhi* — non-apprehension of one of two incompatible items as *liṅga* of the other's presence. *Anvaya-vyāpti* and *vyatireka-vyāpti* are discussed at length, with the five *nyāya-avayava*s (*pratijñā*, *hetu*, *udāharaṇa*, *upanaya*, *nigamana*) and the threefold *liṅga* classification (*kevala-anvayin*, *kevala-vyatirekin*, *anvaya-vyatirekin*). Śrīdhara surveys the full *vyāpti* theory of Vaiśeṣika inference, including the *svārtha-* / *parārtha-anumāna* distinction.
